passage:
Thursday night
Noticed Binita again today. Third week she's eaten lunch on the steps by the library, earphones in, nothing playing (the wire wasn't even plugged in). She used to be all over our class group chat, and now when someone makes a plan, she's never tagged. I don't think anyone's being mean on purpose. People just forgot her, which is kind of worse.
So today I took my tiffin to the steps and sat two steps above, like I just wanted the shade. Asked her if she'd done the geography map. She had. Then I said, "Want to be in our group for the model? We need someone who can draw." She said, "Okay," very fast.
Didn't make a big deal. Nobody noticed. Good.
Tenzin

qa.q: Where has Binita been eating lunch for three weeks?
qa.a: On the steps by the library, earphones in, with nothing playing.

qa.q: Why does Tenzin think people forgetting Binita is "kind of worse"?
qa.a: Tenzin feels that meanness at least gets noticed, while quiet forgetting makes Binita invisible and nobody even sees the need to fix it.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin sit two steps above and ask about the geography map first?
qa.a: Tenzin chose a casual opening so it didn't look like a rescue, which let Binita say yes without feeling singled out.

qa.q: How might the invitation feel from Binita's side?
qa.a: After weeks of not being tagged, being asked because "we need someone who can draw" may feel like being wanted rather than pitied.

grounding: A classmate notices a student eating alone and left out of chats, and includes her in a group task without drawing attention.

passage: In the kasba school, the midday meal was served on the long verandah, and everyone ate in their usual rows. Parveen had noticed that for two weeks Imran, who'd joined when his father took a job at the dairy, sat at the far end by the tap, eating fast and leaving first. When teams formed for the Friday quiz, nobody called his name. Parveen didn't make a speech. On Monday she simply carried her plate to the tap end, "because the shade is better", and asked Imran if he'd got the last sum in the maths homework. He had. On Friday, when Sir told them to form quiz teams, she called out, "Imran's with us," before anyone else could choose. Nobody looked twice. Imran did, though, just once, and nodded.

qa.q: Where did Imran sit to eat his midday meal?
qa.a: At the far end of the verandah, by the tap.

qa.q: Why do you think Parveen said she moved "because the shade is better"?
qa.a: She wanted to sit with Imran without making it look like pity or drawing everyone's attention to him.

qa.q: Which of Parveen's small choices helped most on Friday, and why?
qa.a: Calling "Imran's with us" before teams formed made him part of the group naturally, so he wasn't left to be picked last.

qa.q: What might Imran's single nod say about how Parveen's actions felt to him?
qa.a: It suggests he noticed and was grateful, glad the welcome came quietly without anyone making a scene.

passage: Rania, fifteen, noticed it in her school in Dubai before anyone else seemed to. Aiko, who had moved from Osaka in January, used to sit with a group from art class. Now she ate lunch on the bench by the car park, reading the same page of a book. When Rania checked the class group chat, she saw that a new chat for the art trip had been started, and Aiko wasn't in it. Rania didn't want to make a scene; that would only embarrass Aiko. So on Monday she took her sandwich to the car-park bench and sat at the other end. "Do you know how to shade glass? I'm useless." Aiko looked up. She did know. By Thursday, when Rania's teacher asked students to pick partners for the mural, Rania said, "Aiko and me," before anyone else chose.

qa.q: Where had Aiko started eating lunch?
qa.a: She ate lunch on the bench by the car park.

qa.q: Why did Rania decide not to make a scene?
qa.a: She thought a big fuss would only embarrass Aiko, so she chose a quiet way to include her.

qa.q: Which of Rania's small acts helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking Aiko about shading glass gave her a real reason to talk, and choosing her for the mural included her without drawing attention.

qa.q: How might Aiko feel when Rania picks her for the mural?
qa.a: Aiko would likely feel relieved and wanted, after weeks of eating alone and being left out of the trip chat.

grounding: A teenager notices a classmate eating alone and dropped from a group chat, and includes her through small, quiet acts.

passage: At the chess academy's residential camp, meals were served in a long hall, and the regulars always took the same tables. Jatin, sixteen, noticed that Zainab, the new girl from Hyderabad, had eaten alone for four days, hunched over her pocket chess set. In the camp's group chat, everyone else was tagged in the evening blitz plans; she never was. Jatin didn't announce anything. At breakfast on Friday, he carried his plate to her table and asked, "Can you show me what you did in that endgame yesterday? I couldn't follow it." She could, and explained it with her fork and pepper shaker. That afternoon, when the coach asked students to pair up for analysis, Jatin said, "Zainab and I." Nobody seemed to notice anything unusual. By evening she had been added to the blitz chat.

qa.q: What was Zainab hunched over while eating alone?
qa.a: She was hunched over her pocket chess set.

qa.q: What does Jatin's quiet approach suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted to include Zainab without drawing attention to her loneliness, which might have embarrassed her.

qa.q: Which small act worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking about her endgame and pairing with her for analysis gave Zainab a natural way to join in, which led to her being added to the chat.

qa.q: How might the other campers see Zainab after that day?
qa.a: They may start to see her as part of the group and a strong player, rather than the quiet girl eating alone.

grounding: A teenager notices a new camper eating alone and left out of chats, and includes her through small acts that break the cycle quietly.

passage:
Dear Naveen bhaiya,
You asked if school was better this term. Mostly. But I want to tell you something I noticed.
There's a boy in my class, Raju, who eats alone every day behind the water cooler. Last week I saw he'd been removed from the class group chat; someone made a new one without him. Nobody talked about it. He just stopped coming to the canteen.
I didn't want to make a big thing of it, like standing up in class. So on Monday I sat next to him at lunch and asked about his cricket bat. He looked surprised, then talked for ten minutes. On Wednesday I asked him to be in my project group. Two other guys joined us.
It's small. But he laughed today. I told our class teacher about the group chat too, so she's looking into it.
Vaibhav

qa.q: Where does Raju eat every day?
qa.a: He eats alone every day behind the water cooler.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he noticed Raju had been left out?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt concerned and a little uneasy, wanting to help without drawing attention to Raju.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav's small acts work well?
qa.a: Sitting with Raju and including him in a project broke his isolation quietly, and telling the teacher about the chat brought an adult in.

qa.q: How might Raju feel after Vaibhav sat with him?
qa.a: Raju likely felt surprised and relieved, less lonely, which is why he laughed by the end of the week.

grounding: A student notices a classmate eating alone and dropped from the group chat, and small, quiet acts of inclusion begin to break the cycle.

passage: So, for the school podcast, I'm supposed to talk about kindness. I'm Ira, class ten. There's a girl in our class, Binita, who moved here from Guwahati. For a whole month she ate lunch alone on the steps near the library. I noticed she'd been dropped from our class chat when someone made a new one. Nobody said anything. I felt awful, but I also didn't want to make a scene. So one day I just sat down next to her on the steps with my tiffin. I didn't say "Are you okay?" or anything. I asked what she was reading. It was a mystery novel I liked. Now we eat together most days. Two other girls started joining us. It's not some big rescue. It's just lunch. But she told me last week it was the first time she felt like she belonged here.

qa.q: Where did Binita eat lunch alone?
qa.a: She ate lunch alone on the steps near the library.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when noticing Binita alone?
qa.a: Ira felt awful and concerned, but didn't want to make a scene.

qa.q: What makes Ira's approach effective?
qa.a: Ira simply sat down and asked about the book, a small, low-key act that included Binita without drawing attention.

qa.q: How did Binita experience Ira's small act?
qa.a: Binita felt she belonged for the first time, as she said last week.

grounding: A student notices a classmate eating alone and dropped from the group chat, and a small act of sitting with her breaks the cycle quietly.

passage: I'm Himani, and I sit two rows behind Elizabeth in class eleven. She joined from Shillong in July. By September, I noticed she ate lunch alone at the end of the bench. When the teacher asked us to form project groups, she was always the last one standing. I also noticed she wasn't in the new class chat someone had made. I can't say for sure how she felt. She mostly kept her head down, sometimes reading. But once I saw her check her phone, then put it away quickly, like she'd been hoping for a message. The next time groups were made, I just said, "Elizabeth, join us?" She looked up, surprised, and came over. I added her to the chat that evening. She didn't say much. But she stayed with our group at lunch the next day.

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth eat lunch alone?
qa.a: She ate lunch alone at the end of the bench.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling on seeing Elizabeth check her phone and put it away?
qa.a: Himani felt a pang of sympathy, sensing Elizabeth might be lonely and hoping for a message.

qa.q: Why was a simple "join us?" a good way to help?
qa.a: It included Elizabeth naturally in a task without singling her out, which made it easy for her to accept.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Elizabeth to be asked to join?
qa.a: Elizabeth was surprised and probably relieved, glad not to be the last one standing.

grounding: An observing classmate notices a new student eating alone and left out of chats, and a small invitation to a group breaks the cycle without drawing attention.

passage:
Minakshi, you say there's a girl in your class who always sits alone? Let your Ammamma tell you something. I'm Kavitha. When I was sixteen, there was a girl in our class called Mary. She'd been left out of everything since her father lost his job.
Nobody bullied her. They just forgot her. At lunch she read the same book over and over.
I noticed for weeks. I didn't know what to say. Then one day, in chemistry, the teacher told us to pick lab partners. Everyone paired up fast. Mary stood alone.
I walked over. "Want to be partners?" That's all I said.
We were partners for two years. She came to my wedding.

qa.q: What did Mary read at lunch?
qa.a: She read the same book over and over.

qa.q: What might Kavitha have felt during those weeks of noticing?
qa.a: Kavitha felt uneasy and unsure, noticing Mary's loneliness but not knowing what to say.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Kavitha's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking Mary to be lab partners; it was a small, natural act that didn't draw attention but still included her.

qa.q: How might Mary have felt when Kavitha walked over?
qa.a: Mary likely felt surprised and relieved to be chosen, after weeks of being forgotten.

grounding: Shows, as an elder's memory, a classmate who noticed a lonely girl and broke the cycle with a small invitation to be lab partners.

passage:
It was exam week, and Harish had no time for anything. But he noticed Vishal. Vishal had been dropped from the class study group chat after a fight. At lunch, he sat alone with his notes, not eating.
Harish had a practical exam in twenty minutes. He couldn't have a long talk. So, walking past, he said, "Vishal, the lab needs pairs. You want to be mine?"
Vishal looked up. "Really?"
"Yeah. I'm bad at titration."
In the lab they barely spoke, just passed beakers. But after the exam, Harish added Vishal to his own small revision chat, without saying anything to the class.

qa.q: How long did Harish have before his practical exam?
qa.a: He had a practical exam in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What might Harish have been feeling as he noticed Vishal?
qa.a: He was probably concerned and a bit rushed, wanting to help without much time.

qa.q: What small acts helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking Vishal to be his lab partner and quietly adding him to a revision chat included him without drawing attention.

qa.q: What is it like for Vishal when Harish asks him to be his partner?
qa.a: Vishal feels surprised and relieved, after being left out of the group chat and sitting alone.

grounding: Shows a classmate who notices a student dropped from a group chat and eating alone, and includes him with small, quiet acts despite exam pressure.

passage: "Maria's by herself again," Indu whispered to her friend. "Third day." "She left our group chat, na?" "Did she leave, or did someone remove her?" "Don't know." Indu watched Maria turn the pages of a book she clearly wasn't reading. At the next free period, Indu walked over. "Maria, we're one short for the quiz team. Want to be our science person?" "Me?" "You got full marks in that physics test." Maria hesitated. "Won't the others mind?" "It's my team," Indu said, shrugging. "Practice is after lunch. Just come." Maria nodded, a small smile. After lunch, she came. By the end, she was arguing about Newton with everyone, and nobody remembered she'd been alone.

qa.q: What did Indu ask Maria to be?
qa.a: Their science person on the quiz team.

qa.q: What does Maria's question "Won't the others mind?" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels unsure and unwanted, worried she will be rejected again.

qa.q: How could Indu keep Maria included after the quiz?
qa.a: She could keep inviting her to practices and add her back to the group chat without making a fuss.

qa.q: How does Indu see Maria's situation?
qa.a: Indu sees that Maria has been alone for days and uses a simple task, the quiz team, to include her without drawing attention.

passage: I'm Chandrika, and I'm not proud that it took me three weeks to see it. Madhuri used to sit with our group at lunch. Then one day she was on the bench by the library, alone, with her tiffin on her knees. In the group chat, people started making plans in a new group I later realised she wasn't in. I kept thinking it wasn't my business. Then I saw her laugh at something on her phone, alone, and stop, like she'd remembered where she was. The next day I sat down on the library bench, not saying why. "Can I share your shade?" She moved her bag. We talked about the library's terrible fans. Now I sit there twice a week. It was such a small thing. I should have done it sooner.

qa.q: Where did Madhuri start sitting at lunch?
qa.a: On the bench by the library.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when Chandrika finally sat down?
qa.a: Chandrika felt some regret for waiting three weeks, and quiet concern for Madhuri.

qa.q: What made Chandrika's approach work?
qa.a: It was small and quiet: sitting down and asking to share the shade without drawing attention to Madhuri's loneliness.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel when someone sits on the library bench?
qa.a: Madhuri may feel relieved and less invisible, glad to be sought out without being pitied.

grounding: Illustrates a student noticing a classmate eating alone and dropped from chats, and breaking the cycle with a small act.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 9C, Friday
For two weeks I have noticed Uday eating lunch alone on the steps behind the science block. His friends from last year sit in the canteen. On Wednesday, when I asked the class to check the project details in the class group, Uday said quietly that he wasn't in it any more. He said nothing else, and I didn't press; I didn't want to make a scene. Today I paired him with Nishant and Ishani for the model-making task, both kind and busy students, and put Uday in charge of the circuit, since his wiring was the best in the lab test. By the end of the period the three were arguing happily over a battery. I have added Uday back to the class group myself and will keep an eye on lunchtime.
Tenzin, class teacher

qa.q: Where had Uday been eating lunch?
qa.a: On the steps behind the science block.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin choose not to press Uday for more?
qa.a: Tenzin felt concerned but careful, not wanting to embarrass Uday by turning his loneliness into a scene in front of the class.

qa.q: Why was pairing Uday for the model task a wise step?
qa.a: It included him naturally, with kind classmates and a role using his best skill, breaking the isolation without drawing attention.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Uday to say he wasn't in the group any more?
qa.a: It was probably embarrassing and lonely to admit in front of the class that he had been dropped.

grounding: A teacher notices a student eating alone and dropped from the class group, and quietly includes him in a task where he shines.
